description: We are soil diggeres from Berlin
summary: We built an interactive map and route planner that helps astronauts and mission planners decide where crews can safely travel on Mars, when they can go, and what each trip will cost. The prototype covers about 225 × 200 km of East Melas / Coprates Chasma in Valles Marineris. We chose this region because more high-quality NASA data overlaps there than anywhere else we scored. The map has four aligned layers: Base imagery, Relief, Points of interest, and Weather (static seasonal dust-storm risk). The planner runs on a terrain graph and finds the best route through several destinations for either a suited astronaut or a rover, avoids slopes beyond each one’s limit, and optimises distance and effort as well. Each route reports travel time, oxygen, CO₂, cooling water and energy, scaled to the user’s body mass, and warns about seasonal dust storms.
details:
What does it do, or how does it work?

Our project is a hyper-local interactive map and route planner for astronauts and mission planners. The area is East Melas / Coprates Chasma in Valles  Marineris, about 225 × 200 km. We chose it because it had the most overlapping high-quality data. The map has four layers: 

  1. Base imagery: NASA MRO CTX and HiRISE mosaics from NASA Mars Trek.
  2. Relief and walkability: a 200 m MOLA + HRSC elevation model, turned into slope classes: easy walk, walkable, walkable with caution, vehicle only, and impassable. Clicking any point shows its elevation, slope, and whether it can be walked or driven.
  3. Points of interest: sulfate, silica and hydrous minerals, recurring slope lineae, dune fields, NASA candidate human exploration zones, geology units and place names.
  4. Seasonal dust-storm risk: a 1° grid over the wider Valles Marineris region, computed from 8,428 storms in the Mars Dust Activity Database(1999–2015). Risk is shown separately for each southern-hemisphere season, because an area can be safe in autumn and high-risk in winter.

Behind the map is a multi-destination route planner. The user picks a profile (astronaut or rover), a start point, and several destinations.

The planner returns one path that visits all locations in the best order it finds. It works in three steps:

  1. It builds a terrain graph of about 1.3 million points and 10.3 million directed connections from the elevation model. Uphill and downhill cost differently, and slopes beyond a profile's limit (20° walking, 25° driving) are impassable.
  2.  Shortest paths between every pair of stops, using SciPy's Dijkstra algorithm.
  3.  Destination order, chosen with Google OR-Tools. Stops that can't be reached are dropped and reported with the reason.

Each route reports estimated travel time, oxygen, CO₂, cooling water, and energy. For astronauts, the estimates are recalculated from the logged-in user's body mass. Dust-storm warnings for the chosen season come from the weather layer. In the current version, the route planner runs through the API; the map interface shows the four layers.

What benefits does it have?

  • Multi-mode transportation. Our application supports two profiles: astronaut and rover.
  • Estimated resource consumption per route. After the route is computed, it shows how much oxygen, energy, and water an astronaut would need to complete it.
  • Weather-based warnings for affected routes.
  • One view for planning. Imagery, terrain, science targets, and seasonal hazards are aligned on one map instead of spread across separate tools.
  • Safety-aware routing. Routes avoid slopes that a suited astronaut or a rover can't handle, and report the resources each trip would use.

What is the intended impact?

We want to show how open NASA data can support practical surface operations planning: deciding where crews can safely go, in which season, and what it would cost in oxygen, water, and energy. The project is a working prototype for one region. The same pipeline could cover other landing sites as well.


What tools, languages, hardware, and software did you use?

  • Languages: Python and JavaScript.
  • Backend: FastAPI. NumPy and SciPy (terrain graph, shortest paths, nearest-point lookup). Google OR-Tools (stop ordering). SQLAlchemy with SQLite, plus JWT authentication with Argon2 password hashing (user accounts that store body mass). pytest, with about 470 automated tests, including end-to-end tests on the real data.
  • Frontend: React, Vite, and Leaflet via react-leaflet. Vitest and React Testing Library for tests.
  • Data: NASA Mars Trek (WMTS imagery tiles, ArcGIS image and vector services) and the Mars Dust Activity Database on Harvard Dataverse. A download script fetches everything once.
  • AI assistance: We used Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, to help write code, tests, and documentation.

How is the project creative?

We provide an interactive multi-layered map. It supports multi-destination routing and gives the user the ability to see any number of layers at any time. Other than routing, the user can see resource estimation tailored to the user’s characteristics for a given route. Moreover, we give a user an opportunity to choose a transport mode(astronaut or rover). The route planner finds the path that is cheapest for the chosen transport mode, not just the shortest one. The cost between two points is calculated with the following equation: cost = length × slope margin × (½ × time ratio + ½ × energy ratio).

 What factors did the team consider?

  • Data coverage: we picked the region by scoring how much usable data overlaps there, and kept the weather layer on a wider grid because dust storms are much larger than the area itself.
  • Data reliability: each weather cell is labelled reliable, approximate, or insufficient, based on years observed, number of storms, and whether one extreme year (such as the 2001 global storm) dominates.
  • Physical limits and their sources: the slope limits come from lunar experience, the Artemis suit's stated 20° capability, and the Apollo rover's 25° maximum, because we found no Mars-specific values. Model parameters can be easily configured through a YAML file.
  • Physical constraints: we modelled the astronaut's body mass together with suit and gear mass to estimate the oxygen, CO₂, and cooling water each route needs, and personalised these estimates for each user's body mass. For routing, we considered the Mars terrain: slope limits for walking and driving, the extra cost of going uphill, and seasonal dust-storm risk shown as warnings.
  • Resolution limits: the 200 m elevation model smooths out short, steep features, so all slope values are labelled as approximate.
  • Reliability and repeatability: local static data, automated tests for every module, and a routing graph that rebuilds automatically whenever its source data or settings change.
